power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 37 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (37). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

report: #### MATLAB code, no reproducible output

621 MATLAB code files are present, but this module has no way to extract statistics from MATLAB output, and no self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, a Stata output log, or Mplus output) was found to fall back on. Readers without a MATLAB license cannot currently see what the code produced. Consider depositing the results as well, so they are visible without MATLAB installed: run `diary('output.txt')` (or `diary on`) before the analysis and `diary off` after to save a plain-text transcript of everything printed to the Command Window, or use `publish('script.m', 'pdf')` (or the Live Editor's Export/Save As) to generate a single readable document with the code, its output, and any figures together.

text.text: Search in visual working memory (VWM) is an important process in everyday life, but its computational mechanisms are poorly understood.
Here, we examine whether computational process models from the study of VWM and of visual search also apply to search in VWM.
Participants performed a two-alternative VWM-based color localization task in which we varied set size and color similarity.
We tested models with an encoding stage in which precision is allowed to vary with set size, followed by a Bayesian decision stage.
We found that a variable-precision (VP) model fit the data best, and that adding an item limit did not improve the fit.

We further tested the Target Confusability Competition (TCC) model, which takes a different encoding approach, starting with an empirically established mapping from color distance to discriminability (i.e., the "psychophysical scaling function").
Despite different modeling assumptions, the TCC and VP models produced very similar predictions, with the VP model providing slightly better fits.

To understand this surprising result, we reverse-engineered a psychophysical scaling function from the VP model, and found that it produced a nonlinear mapping similar to the one that TCC defines explicitly.
The VP model's better fits likely stem from its more principled but also less constrained representation of the circular stimulus space.
Finally, we took a resource-rational modeling approach, in which we set mean precision at each set size by optimizing a linear combination of behavioral performance and encoding cost.
A resource-rational model with a power-law cost function captured behavior well, but not better than the best non-resource-rational model.

In sum, a systematic application of computational frameworks from VWM and visual search shows that search in VWM follows patterns very similar to those previously established for search in perception.
However, the effect size of spatial distance was very weak (Fig. 2C).

This is likely because the discrete locations of the stimuli situate 183 them much farther apart.
The only significant interaction was between set size and color distance (F (18, 234) = 3.650, 184 p = .003).
Moving forward, we use color distance and set size as the input variables of our computational models, and 185 do not consider spatial distance.
Visual working memory (VWM) allows individuals to temporarily store, manipulate, and recall information to carry out cognitive tasks.
One category of such tasks entails searching memorized representations of the environment to determine if and where a search target was previously present.
For example, a customer in a grocery store aisle might glance at a display of items in passing and store it in VWM.
If they try to find a specific item upon returning to that aisle a moment later, they might search their memory to now localize that item.
We will refer to this cognitive function as search in visual working memory.

Some studies have explicitly compared search in VWM with visual search (Kuo, Rao, Lepsien, & Nobre, 2009; Eimer & Kiss, 2010; Dell'Acqua, Sessa, Toffanin, Luria, & Jolicœur, 2010; Mazyar, van den Berg, & Ma, 2012; Kong & Fougnie, 2019).
text.formatted: Some studies have explicitly compared search in VWM with visual search <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Kuo, Rao, Lepsien, & Nobre, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Eimer & Kiss, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Dell'Acqua, Sessa, Toffanin, Luria, & Jolicœur, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Mazyar, van den Berg, & Ma, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Kong & Fougnie, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In this visual search literature, a target can be presented before (after) a search array, and is sometimes referred to as a pre-cue (respectively, post-cue).

Search in VWM, as we define it, differs from visual search in that the array is memorized and no longer visible when the search occurs. Kong and Fougnie (2019) found that qualitative effects in visual search-search asymmetries, target-distractor similarity effects, feature versus conjunction benefit, and set size effects-are also present in search in VWM. Mazyar et al. (2012) used a target detection task to directly compare visual search and search in VWM, and found that set size effects were similar in both-accuracy decreased with set size when distractors were heterogeneous, regardless of whether the array was visible or memorized.

(2012)</ref> used a target detection task to directly compare visual search and search in VWM, and found that set size effects were similar in both-accuracy decreased with set size when distractors were heterogeneous, regardless of whether the array was visible or memorized.

text.text: Additionally, EEG studies have identified neural signatures of target detection in VWM that are similar to those in visual search, specifically the presence of the N2pc component (Kuo et al., 2009; Eimer & Kiss, 2010; Dell'Acqua et al., 2010).

text.text: While search in VWM is naturally viewed in relation to visual search, its connections to aspects of VWM are also theoretically interesting.
We distinguish search in VWM from standard VWM tasks, where a probe specifies which item to retrieve, so that the retrieval process reduces to reading out a single feature from memory.
In search in VWM, the probe does not directly identify the item, and the observer must search their memorized array to find the item matching the probe.

This puts search in VWM in contact with a separate VWM literature on retro-cues (Astle, Summerfield, Griffin, & Nobre, 2012; Griffin & Nobre, 2003; Rerko, Souza, & Oberauer, 2014), in which a spatial cue presented after array offset but before the test probe directs attention to a subset of memorized items, allowing observers to selectively prioritize those representations.
text.formatted: This puts search in VWM in contact with a separate VWM literature on retro-cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Astle, Summerfield, Griffin, & Nobre, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Griffin & Nobre, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Rerko, Souza, & Oberauer, 2014)</ref>, in which a spatial cue presented after array offset but before the test probe directs attention to a subset of memorized items, allowing observers to selectively prioritize those representations.

text.text: These studies probe the limits of selective attention within VWM.

In this paper, our task does not entail a spatial cue which pre-specifies the target location, but instead the observer must compare the probe against all stored representations simultaneously-making search in VWM a window into the limits of distributed attention over memory, rather than selective attention to a known item.
The study of visual search and the study of visual working memory have benefited greatly from computational modeling.

In both domains, it has long been known that encoding is noisy and that the amount of noise increases with set size (visual search: (Shaw, 1978; Palmer, 1994; Mazyar et al., 2012); VWM: (Wilken & Ma, 2004; Bays & Husain, 2008)).
text.formatted: In both domains, it has long been known that encoding is noisy and that the amount of noise increases with set size (visual search: <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Shaw, 1978;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Palmer, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Mazyar et al., 2012)</ref>; VWM: <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">(Wilken & Ma, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Bays & Husain, 2008)</ref>).

text.text: In the study of VWM, models with this kind of noise are often called resource models, since the precision associated with the noise can be thought of as an encoding resource (Bays, 2015).
text.formatted: In the study of VWM, models with this kind of noise are often called resource models, since the precision associated with the noise can be thought of as an encoding resource <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bays, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Resource models, augmented where needed with a Bayesian decision stage, provide excellent accounts of human behavior across a wide range of paradigms: delayed estimation (Bays & Husain, 2008; Bays, Catalao, & Husain, 2009; van den Berg, Shin, Chou, George, & Ma, 2012; Fougnie, Suchow, & Alvarez, 2012; van den Berg, Awh, & Ma, 2014; Taylor & Bays, 2018a), change detection (Wilken & Ma, 2004; Keshvari, van den Berg, & Ma, 2013 , 2012), and change localization (van den Berg et al., 2012; D. T. Devkar, Wright, & Ma, 2015; D. Devkar, Wright, & Ma, 2017).

T. <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Devkar, Wright, & Ma, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">D. Devkar, Wright, & Ma, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, most of these studies (but see (van den Berg et al., 2014)) found no benefit of postulating either an additional limit on the number of items (Luck & Vogel, 1997; Cowan, 2000) or a discrete number of resource "chunks" (Zhang & Luck, 2008).
text.formatted: Moreover, most of these studies (but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(van den Berg et al., 2014)</ref>) found no benefit of postulating either an additional limit on the number of items <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Luck & Vogel, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Cowan, 2000)</ref> or a discrete number of resource "chunks" <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">(Zhang & Luck, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Another account of VWM behavior that rejects item limits is provided by the Target Confusability Competition (TCC) model (Schurgin, Wixted, & Brady, 2020).
text.formatted: Another account of VWM behavior that rejects item limits is provided by the Target Confusability Competition (TCC) model <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Schurgin, Wixted, & Brady, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Like resource models, TCC assumes noisy encoding, but it characterizes the noise indirectly through an empirically measured function that captures how the perceived similarity between two stimuli changes nonlinearly with stimulus distance.
Prior work has started to compare resource models with the TCC model.

One study noted that the TCC and VP models can make qualitatively similar predictions in the context of swap errors, as both attribute large memory errors to noisy item-based responses rather than to guessing (Williams, Robinson, & Brady, 2023).
text.formatted: One study noted that the TCC and VP models can make qualitatively similar predictions in the context of swap errors, as both attribute large memory errors to noisy item-based responses rather than to guessing <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">(Williams, Robinson, & Brady, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, whether this convergence reflects shared underlying computational principles between the two modeling approaches remains an open question.

Two studies have begun to address this. Bays (2019); Tomić and Bays (2024) compared TCC to the neural resource model, a population-coding account of working memory in which a stimulus is encoded by a population of noisy neurons.
text.formatted: Two studies have begun to address this. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Bays (2019)</ref>; <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Tomić and Bays (2024)</ref> compared TCC to the neural resource model, a population-coding account of working memory in which a stimulus is encoded by a population of noisy neurons.

text.text: The authors argue that TCC and the neural resource model are built the same way: in both, a stimulus produces a response that is strongest when a candidate value matches the true stimulus, and weaker for candidate values farther away, and this response is corrupted by noise to produce an estimate.

They argue that the only difference between TCC and the neural resource model is the specific function describing how the response weakens with distance-an empirically measured similarity function in TCC, versus a fixed bell-shaped curve in the neural resource model.

On this basis, the authors conclude that TCC's success comes by way of its architecturea noisy response that decays with distance and is then decoded-rather than from the specific empirical similarity function it plugs into that architecture. Tomić and Bays (2024) found supporting evidence for this in two ways.
text.formatted: On this basis, the authors conclude that TCC's success comes by way of its architecturea noisy response that decays with distance and is then decoded-rather than from the specific empirical similarity function it plugs into that architecture. <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Tomić and Bays (2024)</ref> found supporting evidence for this in two ways.

text.text: First, letting the shape of the response function be freely fit to memory data, rather than fixed to match separately measured perceptual similarity judgments, produced a fit that was as good as or better than using the true empirical similarity function.
Second, using a generic bell-shaped (von Mises) function performed just as well as TCC's own empirical function.
The authors tested this across four feature spaces (color, orientation, angular location, and shape), using a visual working memory analogue report task as their measure of memory performance.

However, the authors treat the response of a whole population of neurons as equivalent to the response of a single neuron, and this assumption may limit the generalizability of their findings because the discriminability of two stimuli, as computed from a full population of neurons, is not the same quantity as the response of one neuron to those stimuli (Carney, Paradiso, & Freeman, 1989; Seung & Sompolinsky, 1993; Ma, 2010).

text.text: Thus, whether TCC and resource models actually share a common computational framework about how memory errors arise remains an open question.
While search in VWM sits at the intersection of visual search and of VWM, computational modeling in this domain has been somewhat limited.

This is partly because most experimental designs have used letters, complex shapes, and naturalistic objects as stimuli (Kong & Fougnie, 2019; Kuo et al., 2009; Dell'Acqua et al., 2010; Eimer & Kiss, 2010).
text.formatted: This is partly because most experimental designs have used letters, complex shapes, and naturalistic objects as stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Kong & Fougnie, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Kuo et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Dell'Acqua et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Eimer & Kiss, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Such stimuli are hard to vary in a systematic, controlled way, which makes computational modeling difficult.

There are notable exceptions (Schneegans & Bays, 2016 , 2017; Mazyar et al., 2012; Bays, 2014; Tomić & Bays, 2024), which used stimuli that varied continuously along one or more feature dimensions, allowing quantitative model fitting. Schneegans and Bays (2016) had observers report the remembered location of a color-cued item in a two-dimensional pointing task.

text.text: They found that recall variability rose monotonically with set size, and that accounting for swap errors removed the apparent guessing a slot model predicts -consistent with a resource account rather than a fixed item limit.
Response latency rose monotonically with set size as well, which speaks to the search process itself.

The same populationcoding framework gives a mechanistic basis for these effects, since normalized population activity leaves each added item encoded with less activity, producing noisier recall as set size grows (Bays, 2014). Schneegans and Bays (2017) extended this model with conjunctive coding to account for swap errors as binding failures.

text.text: In these studies, though, the response was a continuous location estimate.

For search in VWM this is an unnecessary complication, since error can arise in pinpointing location even when color is remembered perfectly. Mazyar et al. (2012) avoided continuous report with a target detection task, comparing Bayesian observers whose precision was fixed or set-size dependent, and equal or variable across items.
text.formatted: For search in VWM this is an unnecessary complication, since error can arise in pinpointing location even when color is remembered perfectly. <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Mazyar et al. (2012)</ref> avoided continuous report with a target detection task, comparing Bayesian observers whose precision was fixed or set-size dependent, and equal or variable across items.

text.text: They found that precision fell with set size, and that distractor variability rather than memory demand drove the effect.
But the present-or-absent decision depended on a criterion as well as precision, so the prior probability of target presence had to be fit as a free parameter.
A two-alternative forced-choice task with two equally likely options removes this -the optimal decision is simply to pick the option with greater evidence.
With no free parameter at the decision stage, encoding precision becomes the only source of set-size effects, and any set-size dependence can be attributed directly to encoding.
The present study builds on this work and extends it modestly in several ways.
Compared to Schneegans and Bays (2016, 2017), we chose stimuli that vary along a single feature dimension (color) and placed them at highly distinct locations.
text.formatted: Compared to <ref type="bibr">Schneegans and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Bays (2016, 2017)</ref>, we chose stimuli that vary along a single feature dimension (color) and placed them at highly distinct locations.

text.text: Therefore, the difficulty of search in VWM is predominantly a function of feature encoding.
Compared to Mazyar et al. (2012), we use target localization instead of target detection and color instead of orientation.
text.formatted: Compared to <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Mazyar et al. (2012)</ref>, we use target localization instead of target detection and color instead of orientation.

text.text: Compared to all three prior studies, we test a much wider set of models.
We start with earlier resource models of VWM that consist of a noisy encoding stage and a Bayesian decision stage (Keshvari et al., 2013; van den Berg et al., 2012; Keshvari et al., 2012).
text.formatted: We start with earlier resource models of VWM that consist of a noisy encoding stage and a Bayesian decision stage <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Keshvari et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">van den Berg et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Keshvari et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Our models vary along two dimensions: whether precision is equal or variable across items and trials, and whether there is an item limit.
We ask whether a non-parametric account of set size effects matches the behavior of the best parametric model.
We then formally compare the resource models to the TCC model, and ask whether the nonlinear psychophysical scaling emphasized by TCC is implicitly present in the resource models.
Finally, we test whether resource-rational accounts capture set size effects in search and VWM.
While resource and TCC models generally account well for search behavior, they do not postulate an underlying mechanism for the decrease of encoding precision with increasing set size.
Resource-rational models can address this shortcoming.

Such models postulate that the brain performs an optimal computation while being bound by biological or cognitive constraints on either the encoding or the decision stage (Simon, 1957; Attwell & Laughlin, 2001; Lennie, 2003; Griffiths, Lieder, & Goodman, 2015; Bhui, Lai, & Gershman, 2021).
text.formatted: Such models postulate that the brain performs an optimal computation while being bound by biological or cognitive constraints on either the encoding or the decision stage <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Simon, 1957;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Attwell & Laughlin, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Lennie, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Griffiths, Lieder, & Goodman, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Bhui, Lai, & Gershman, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: While van den Berg and Ma (2018) introduced the notion of resource rationality in the study of VWM, it remains untested whether a resource-rational model can capture set size effects in search; we also ask this question here.

text.text: Fourteen participants performed our experiment after providing informed consent.
The experiment conformed to the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) at Baylor College of Medicine, W.J.M.'s previous institution.
The stimuli were presented on a Dell 1907FPC LCD monitor, with a refresh rate of 75 Hz.
The participant was seated approximately 60 cm from the monitor.
Throughout the experiment, the screen background was kept a uniform gray, with a luminance of 8.1 cd/m 2.
Each memory array consisted of 2, 4, 6 or 8 circular, colored discs (i.e., the stimuli).

Stimuli could appear at 8 possible locations, placed equidistantly on an imaginary circle of radius 4.5 degrees of visual angle centered at the fixation point; thus, if two stimuli were adjacently located, they were 45 • apart along the circle.
The color of each stimulus lay on a circle in the uniform CIELAB color space with a constant lightness value of L = 70.
The center of the circle was (a = 10, b = 10) and its radius was 75.

On this circle, 180 colors were chosen at angles {2 • , 4 • , . . . , 360 • }, so that neighboring colors had an angular color distance of 2 • ; these were the possible color values for all stimuli in the experiment.
For experimental display, we converted CIELAB values to RGB values via an intermediate CIE XYZ color space (León, Mery, Pedreschi, & León, 2006).
text.formatted: For experimental display, we converted CIELAB values to RGB values via an intermediate CIE XYZ color space <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(León, Mery, Pedreschi, & León, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: On each trial, we chose a target and a non-target color while constructing the memory array.
The target color was uniformly sampled from the 180 possible color values.
The non-target color was computed by adding a predetermined angular color distance to the target color (measured along the circle in CIELAB space).
This distance was uniformly sampled from 40 values equally spaced between -175.5 • and 175.5 • (thus not containing 0 • ), which we rounded to the closest 2 • .
Colors other than the target and the non-target color were uniformly sampled from the 180 possible color values.
At the start of a trial, the participant fixated on a centrally presented white cross for 1000 ms (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: At the start of a trial, the participant fixated on a centrally presented white cross for 1000 ms (Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: The memory array was then presented for 100 ms.
Next, during a delay period lasting 1000 ms, only the fixation cross was shown.

The participant then viewed a probe array, which was almost identical to the memory array, except that two discs from the memory array were replaced by light-gray circular outlines; moreover, one of the two "missing" colors (the target color) was presented in a small disc at the center of the screen.
We will refer to the other missing color as the non-target color/stimulus.
The participant then reported the remembered location of the target stimulus by clicking inside one of the two gray outlines.
There was no time limit on the response.
The experiment began with a demonstration video on how to perform the task.

Then, each participant was given a practice round with a minimum of 10 trials, after which the participant could choose when to proceed to the testing trials of the experiment-provided they had achieved at least 60% accuracy during practice.
We used a factorial design over set size, spatial target-non-target distance, and color target-non-target distance, for a total of 4 × 4 ×40 = 640 trial types.
Each trial type was presented once, for a total of 640 trials per participant.
The order of the 640 trials was randomized and they were subsequently divided into 5 blocks of 128 trials each.
Feedback on the proportion of correct responses was provided after each block.
The participant could take a break after each block.
We first analyzed proportion correct as a function of set size, color distance and spatial distance between the target and the non-target (Fig. 2).
text.formatted: We first analyzed proportion correct as a function of set size, color distance and spatial distance between the target and the non-target (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>).

To model the decision stage, we use Bayesian inference.
Bayesian models are principled because the Bayesian observer uses their knowledge of the generative model in a way that maximizes accuracy or minimizes a cost.

Moreover, models with a Bayesian decision stage have a long track record of describing decisions in both visual search (Ma, Navalpakkam, Beck, van den Berg, & Pouget, 2011; Mazyar et al., 2012; Ma, Shen, Dziugaite, & van den Berg, 2015; Mihali & Ma, 2020) and VWM (Keshvari et al., 2012; van den Berg et al., 2012; D. T. Devkar et al., 2015).

text.text: The encoding stage describes how the stimuli are represented internally by the observer by defining the noise distribution and the properties of the associated precision.
In addition, we ask if there is a fixed number of items that humans can encode.

A classic question in the VWM literature is whether VWM performance is limited by a fixed number of items that can be stored (item-limit models) (Pashler, 1988; Zhang & Luck, 2008; Adam, Vogel, & Awh, 2017; Cowan, 2001), or by encoding noise-the precision of which depends on set size (resource models) (Wilken & Ma, 2004; Lakha & Wright, 2004; Bays & Husain, 2008; Oberauer, 2022).

For each model and each participant, we ran BADS with 20 starting points and chose the best-fitting parameters among those.
We took the logarithm of J1 , α and τ before fitting.
We chose the plausible ranges to be [log(0.01), log(600)] for log J1 , [log(0.01), log(5)] for log α, and [log(0.01), log(600)] for log τ .
The model's fit is not governed by any parameter's individual value, but by how the parameters jointly combine to minimize the NLL value.
This means that multiple combinations of parameters might lead to the same NLL value-making them indistinguishable to the fitting procedure.
As a result, we do not interpret parameter estimate values.

We compared models using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) (Akaike, 1974), the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) (Schwarz, 1978) and cross-validation (Evans, Howard, Heathcote, & Brown, 2017).

text.text: AIC and BIC are defined as AIC = -2 • LL* + 2n parameters and BIC = -2 • LL* + n parameters log n trials , respectively, where LL* is the maximum log likelihood and n parameters is the number of free parameters.
We performed 5-fold cross-validation, stratified by set size and color distance, and summed the cross-validated negative log likelihood across all the folds.
We repeated this procedure for 100 random partitions of the data.
All cross-validation results can be found in the Appendix.
For each participant, we computed the metric (AIC/BIC/cross-validated negative log likelihood) difference of each model relative to the best-fitting model.
We report the sum across participants, as well as a 95% bootstrapped confidence interval on this sum (using 10 5 bootstrap samples).
Summing the differences in the metrics across participants relies on the assumption that all participants are fitted best by the same model.
Model comparison indicates which candidate model performs best relative to the others, but it does not establish whether the winning model adequately reproduces the observed data.
We therefore conducted model checks.
For each participant, we used the fitted model and parameter estimates to simulate 10,000 responses per trial.
We processed these simulated responses using the same summary and aggregation procedures applied to the observed data.
We then visually compared the model predictions with the observed data, treating overlap between their SEM bands as a descriptive indication of fit.
So far, we have assumed that both the target and the non-target stimulus are always encoded in memory.
However, an old idea in the study of VWM is that only a limited number of stimuli (items) can be stored (Pashler, 1988; Cowan, 2001; Luck & Vogel, 1997).

Thus far, the decision rule specified in our modeling methodology assumes that the observers have access to the specific precision with which the stimulus was encoded.

Relying on a decision rule in which the observer has access to the specific precisions with which the stimuli are encoded has been a common and successful assumption in theories of cue combination (Serwe, Körding, & Trommershäuser, 2011) and other forms of probabilistic computation (Adler & Ma, 2018; Ma et al., 2011; Qamar et al., 2013; Denison, Adler, Carrasco, & Ma, 2018).

text.text: In this paper, we take a principled modeling approach to search in VWM.
Our main findings are threefold.
First, several Bayesian observer models accounted for behavior in this task reasonably well, showing that computational frameworks from visual search and VWM extend naturally to search in VWM.
Second, the variable-precision (VP) model provided the best overall account of behavior, even after penalizing for model complexity, with no need for assuming additional item limits.

These results fit with previous work on resource limitations in visual search (Mazyar et al., 2012; Mihali & Ma, 2020) and visual working memory (Ma et al., 2014; Bays & Husain, 2008; Fougnie et al., 2012; Mazyar et al., 2012; Mazyar, van den Berg, Seilheimer, & Ma, 2013; van den Berg et al., 2012; D. T. Devkar et al., 2015; Bays, Schneegans, Ma, & Brady, 2024).

T. Devkar et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Bays, Schneegans, Ma, & Brady, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, our results show that a Bayesian observer framework in which precision decreases with set size extends naturally to search in VWM.
Interestingly, we also found that the Target Confusability Competition (TCC) model produced very similar predictions to those of the VP model despite its different modeling assumptions.
Third, a resource-rational modeling approach, which derived encoding precision from a trade-off between neural and behavioral cost, was unable to outperform the VP model.
To reach these conclusions, we applied computational approaches from visual search and VWM to a new memory-based localization task.

We tested Bayesian observer models with different encoding stages and decision rules, ranging from resource models to more normative resource-rational models that imposed stronger constraints on how an observer should allocate encoding resources.
This comparison allowed us to ask not only which model fit behavior best, but also whether different theoretical modeling commitments actually lead to different empirical predictions.
Our comparison of the TCC model with our best-performing VP model opened a new avenue of exploration.
We delved deeper into the differences between the TCC and VP models and asked what distinguishes them conceptually.
Although the two models appear to make different assumptions, we found that they arrive at very similar predictions.
TCC makes psychophysical scaling explicit, whereas VP does not.
However, in practice, the explicit psychophysical scaling in TCC appears to be implicitly approximated in VP through its assumption of circular color distance.
Thus, despite their different formulations, the two models may capture similar underlying structure.
Consistent with this idea, our reverse-engineering analysis showed that the VP model, re-expressed in terms of effective d ′ , produces discriminability patterns similar to those of the TCC model.

A related question has been asked before in the context of a different resource model, the neural resource model (Bays, 2014) Bays (2019); Tomić and Bays (2024)argued that TCC and the neural resource model share a common underlying architecture.
text.formatted: A related question has been asked before in the context of a different resource model, the neural resource model <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bays, 2014)</ref> <ref type="formula">Bays (2019); Tomić and Bays (2024)</ref>argued that TCC and the neural resource model share a common underlying architecture.

text.text: We were able to extend their hypothesis by comparing TCC with a different resource model, the VP model.
Importantly, we compared them using proportion correct, a quantity that is well-defined across feature spaces, including the circular geometry of color spaces used in our task.
Next, we asked whether the observed precision patterns can also be explained as the result of a normative resourceallocation principle.
To address this, we tested a resource-rational version of the VP model, in which encoding precision is derived from minimizing a combination of behavioral cost and neural cost.
This model performed well, but only after adding an arbitrary power-law parameter to the resource cost function.
The basic VP model, its non-parametric variant, and its best resource-rational variant all indicated a decrease in mean precision with set size that approximated a power law.
At the same time, these results do not provide a strong test of the resource-rational framework in general.
Adding the cost-function parameter effectively shifts flexibility from one power law governing precision to another power law governing cost.
Stronger tests could be conducted in future work by including more set sizes or by obtaining an independent measure of the cost of precision.
Our results are qualitatively very similar to previous patterns established for search in perception (Kuo et al., 2009; Kong & Fougnie, 2019; Mihali & Ma, 2020).
text.formatted: Our results are qualitatively very similar to previous patterns established for search in perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Kuo et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Kong & Fougnie, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Mihali & Ma, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These studies showed that accuracy decreased with increasing set size and with increasing target-distractor similarity in both perception and memory.
Our work approached the same question using precise psychophysical measurements and computational modeling.
Measuring neural activity in both conditions could further refine this account.

In delayed localization, Li, Sprague, Yoo, Ma, and Curtis (2021, 2025) showed that VWM content and uncertainty are jointly encoded in early visual cortex, and that neural activity during the delay period predicts behavioral performance.
text.formatted: In delayed localization, <ref type="bibr">Li, Sprague, Yoo, Ma, and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Curtis (2021, 2025)</ref> showed that VWM content and uncertainty are jointly encoded in early visual cortex, and that neural activity during the delay period predicts behavioral performance.

text.text: A natural extension would be to ask whether the same neural representations that support perceptual search also support search in VWM.
A related open question is whether search in VWM proceeds serially or in parallel.
Previous work has suggested that response times increasing with set size imply serial scanning of memory, as in Sternberg (1966)'s classic detection task with discrete symbols.
text.formatted: Previous work has suggested that response times increasing with set size imply serial scanning of memory, as in <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Sternberg (1966)</ref>'s classic detection task with discrete symbols.

text.text: Our task shares the same basic structure-participants encode a set of items, then use a probe to search memory and make a binary response-and we too find that response times increase approximately linearly with set size (Appendix 5).
However, Sternberg's paradigm used easily discriminable stimuli that minimized representational uncertainty, bringing them closer to investigating the temporal dynamics of retrieval.
Our task uses continuous visual features, and performance depends not just on whether retrieval occurred but on the precision of noisy memory representations.
Our models are built to capture this precision-dependent component, not retrieval speed.
The linear response time increase is therefore consistent with, but does not by itself imply, serial search.

Distinguishing serial from parallel search in VWM would require paradigms that more directly target retrieval dynamics, for example by combining response time measurements with eye tracking or by manipulating the temporal structure of the search process.
Another possible future direction comes from the fact that here we have only approached one way in which visual search and VWM interact.
Throughout, we have treated search in VWM as a self-contained task: an observer holds a set of items in memory and searches that memory for a match to an external probe.
The reverse relationship also occurs during ordinary visual search of an external display, where an observer holds a target template in memory and uses it to guide search through the visual array.

This is straightforward when the target is fixed, but becomes more demanding when the target varies from trial to trial (Chelazzi, Miller, Duncan, & Desimone, 1993; Carlisle, Arita, Pardo, & Woodman, 2011; Goldstein & Beck, 2018), or when irrelevant features of the target are encoded alongside the relevant one (Olivers, Peters, Houtkamp, & Roelfsema, 2011; Hollingworth & Beck, 2016; van Moorselaar, Theeuwes, & Olivers, 2014).
text.formatted: This is straightforward when the target is fixed, but becomes more demanding when the target varies from trial to trial <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Chelazzi, Miller, Duncan, & Desimone, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Carlisle, Arita, Pardo, & Woodman, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Goldstein & Beck, 2018)</ref>, or when irrelevant features of the target are encoded alongside the relevant one <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Olivers, Peters, Houtkamp, & Roelfsema, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Hollingworth & Beck, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">van Moorselaar, Theeuwes, & Olivers, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In these cases, the precision with which the target template is maintained in memory should directly affect search performance, much as memory precision determined performance in our task.

This suggests that the same computational framework used here, namely precision decreasing with set size and search performance governed by noisy memory representations, may extend to template-guided search as well.
Lastly, our experiment is simplified in several ways.
First, it manipulates only two stimulus dimensions-location and color-and the range of variation within each dimension is limited.
For example, stimuli can appear in only eight possible locations, all positioned at a fixed distance from the central fixation point.
This limits the generalizability of our findings.

One approach to increase ecological validity in experimental design would be to use more naturalistic stimuli such as real-world objects or photographs (Brady, Konkle, Gill, Oliva, & Alvarez, 2013; Bates, Lerch, Sims, & Jacobs, 2019), but doing so increases stimulus complexity while leaving the task structure largely unchanged.
text.formatted: One approach to increase ecological validity in experimental design would be to use more naturalistic stimuli such as real-world objects or photographs <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Brady, Konkle, Gill, Oliva, & Alvarez, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Bates, Lerch, Sims, & Jacobs, 2019)</ref>, but doing so increases stimulus complexity while leaving the task structure largely unchanged.

text.text: A second approach would be to increase the complexity of the task itself.

In the real world, items may differ in value or behavioral relevance, and observers may combine perceptual and reward information to decide what to search for (Navalpakkam, Koch, Rangel, & Perona, 2010).
text.formatted: In the real world, items may differ in value or behavioral relevance, and observers may combine perceptual and reward information to decide what to search for <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Navalpakkam, Koch, Rangel, & Perona, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Real search may also involve unpredictable item positions, visual clutter, and time pressure, none of which our paradigm imposed.

Furthermore, real-world scenarios in which people search memory involve structured scenes rather than arbitrary arrays, bringing in semantic and spatial regularities that constrain where targets are likely to be found (Võ & Wolfe, 2015).
text.formatted: Furthermore, real-world scenarios in which people search memory involve structured scenes rather than arbitrary arrays, bringing in semantic and spatial regularities that constrain where targets are likely to be found <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Võ & Wolfe, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Incorporating any of these elements into laboratory paradigms for search in VWM could make those paradigms more relevant to real-world search, and testing whether the computational models studied here generalize to these richer conditions would be a natural extension of this work.

text.text: This work introduced a simple two-alternative forced-choice paradigm to measure search in visual working memory (VWM), and adapted existing computational frameworks from VWM and visual search to the resulting behavior.
Our best-fitting model consisted of a variable precision encoding scheme and a Bayesian decision stage, with no benefit of adding an item limit.
Applying the Target Confusability Competition model with its explicit incorporation of the psychophysical scaling framework did not provide a better fit to our data.
Conceptually, we found that the VP framework and TCC framework have distinct but ultimately comparable ways of incorporating nonlinearities in stimulus distance.

Lastly, a resource-rational variant of the VP model, in which mean precision was derived from a trade-off between behavioral and encoding cost, captured behavior well but did not outperform the standard VP model.

text.text: The VP model, however, does not postulate such a function.
How can it then still generate qualitatively similar fits and even perform quantitatively a little better than the TCC model?
We claim that while the nonlinearity is not manually constructed in the VP model, it is implicitly present.
The central quantity in the TCC model is d ′ , which assumes Gaussian distributions over the internal representations of stimuli.

While this is a common assumption in the psychophysics literature and could be justified if "internal representation" is defined sufficiently abstractly, it is not grounded in the physical stimulus space.
In our task, as in the tasks used by Schurgin et al. (2020), color space is circular.
text.formatted: In our task, as in the tasks used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Schurgin et al. (2020)</ref>, color space is circular.

text.text: However, the TCC model is a signal detection theory model and thus assumes Gaussian noise, which does not respect the circular geometry of color space.
By contrast, in the VP model, measurement noise is defined directly in circular space (via the von Mises distribution).
The circular nature of the space is carried through both the generative model and the (cosine-based) decision rule.
Therefore, it is possible that in the VP model, a nonlinear relationship between stimulus distance and discriminability emerges without separately positing an explicit similarity mapping.
To show that this is indeed the case, we "reverse engineered" d ′ values from the VP model's predicted proportion correct per participant.
Recall that we denoted by f (d ′ ) the mapping from d ′ to proportion correct in our task within an SDT framework (Equation 26).
text.formatted: Recall that we denoted by f (d ′ ) the mapping from d ′ to proportion correct in our task within an SDT framework (Equation <ref type="formula">26</ref>).

text.text: This mapping only depended on the task and on the basic SDT assumptions of Equations 24 and 25, and not on any of the specific assumptions of either the TCC or the VP model.

We first calculated this mapping numerically for a fine grid of d ′ values ∈ [0, 8]; for each value of d ′ , we drew 200,000 samples of x 1 ∼ N (0, 1) and x 2 ∼ N (d ′ , 1), and calculated the proportion of these samples for which |x 2 | > |x 1 |.
text.formatted: We first calculated this mapping numerically for a fine grid of d ′ values ∈ [0, 8]; for each value of d ′ , we drew 200,000 samples of x 1 ∼ N (0, 1) and x 2 ∼ N (d ′ , 1), and calculated the proportion of these samples for which |x 2 | > |x 1 |.

text.text: Then, for each combination of color distance, set size, and participant, we took proportion correct as predicted by the fitted VP model and converted it to a d ′ value using our numerical approximation to f and one-dimensional linear interpolation (MATLAB's interp1).

The resulting values are interpretable as discriminability values, even though the concept of discriminability is not part of the VP model per se; therefore, we call it "effective discriminability" or "effective d ′ ."
As we hypothesized, we found that the VP model implicitly contains a nonlinear mapping between discriminability and color distance (Figure 9B).
text.formatted: As we hypothesized, we found that the VP model implicitly contains a nonlinear mapping between discriminability and color distance (Figure <ref type="figure">9B</ref>).

text.text: Moreover, the TCC and VP models yielded qualitatively similar d ′ patterns (Figure 9A vs B).
text.formatted: Moreover, the TCC and VP models yielded qualitatively similar d ′ patterns (Figure <ref type="figure">9A</ref> vs B).

text.text: However, under the VP model, the effective d ′ curves across set sizes were not simply scaled multiples of one another.
This suggests that the scaling assumption built into the TCC model may be restrictive, potentially explaining why the TCC model fits the behavioral data slightly worse overall than the VP model.

text.text: In this neural resource model of working memory (Bays, 2014), a population of independent Poisson neurons encodes a memorized stimulus, with gain inversely proportional to set size.
text.formatted: In this neural resource model of working memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bays, 2014)</ref>, a population of independent Poisson neurons encodes a memorized stimulus, with gain inversely proportional to set size.

text.text: The authors note that d ′ can be naturally derived from such a model.
To obtain the dependence of d ′ on set size, they further note that d ′ scales with the square root of neural gain and thus inversely with the square root of set size.
To obtain the dependence of d ′ on stimulus distance, the authors use the von Mises tuning curve of a single neuron directly as the functional form.

This is somewhat puzzling, because the discriminability of two stimuli based on a population is not identical to that based on a single neuron (Carney et al., 1989; Seung & Sompolinsky, 1993; Ma, 2010).
text.formatted: This is somewhat puzzling, because the discriminability of two stimuli based on a population is not identical to that based on a single neuron <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Carney et al., 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Seung & Sompolinsky, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Ma, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: To obtain the population-based discriminability, one would have to either simulate the neural responses to the stimulus pairs used in the experiment or use the (analytical) distribution of maximum-likelihood estimates of the stimuli based on the neural activity (Ma, 2010).
text.formatted: To obtain the population-based discriminability, one would have to either simulate the neural responses to the stimulus pairs used in the experiment or use the (analytical) distribution of maximum-likelihood estimates of the stimuli based on the neural activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Ma, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The latter approach would reduce to our "reverse engineering" process, with our measurement x of a stimulus identified with the maximumlikelihood estimate of that stimulus based on the neural response, which is standard practice in population coding models (Ma, 2010).
text.formatted: The latter approach would reduce to our "reverse engineering" process, with our measurement x of a stimulus identified with the maximumlikelihood estimate of that stimulus based on the neural response, which is standard practice in population coding models <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Ma, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In either approach, it would be obvious that the decision is made in a circular space and therefore, the standard signal detection theory formalism and the standard definition of d ′ , which assume Gaussian noise on the real line, do not apply.

It is exactly for this reason that in the VP model, we calculated proportion correct, which is well-defined in any space, and only reverse-engineered an effective d ′ to facilitate comparison with the TCC model.

In sum, the d ′ comparison between the TCC model and the neural resource model by Tomić and Bays (2024), if done correctly, would look very similar to the comparison between the TCC model and the VP model presented here.

text.text: Following van den Berg and Ma (2018), who found evidence for resource-rational behavior in some VWM tasks, we aim to understand whether behavior in search in VWM is also resource-rational.
